author: NorthEast News Desk
body: A Hong Kong court sentenced two former leaders of the group that organized the city’s annual Tiananmen Square vigils to prison terms of at least seven years Friday, the latest major ruling under the territory’s national security law.

Lee Cheuk-yan, 69, received seven years, while Chow Hang-tung, 41, received seven years and three months after their convictions for inciting subversion. Both had pleaded not guilty and have been in custody since 2021, Reuters reported.

Albert Ho, 74, another former chairman of the now-disbanded Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, pleaded guilty in January and was sentenced to five years and two months. The court also imposed a HK$1.5 million fine on the alliance.

The group organized public commemorations of Beijing’s 1989 crackdown for years, when such gatherings were legal in Hong Kong. Those vigils were effectively halted after the security law took effect in 2020. The sentences are developing news because any appeals, defense responses or further court action had not been announced in the initial report.
dek: Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung were sentenced under the national security law after convictions tied to a disbanded group’s pro-democracy activities.
headline: Hong Kong court gives Tiananmen vigil leaders seven-year terms
